description: We’re Fire Computer, a team of six who love space, data and building tools people actually enjoy using. Between us we bring skills in data science and Python, geospatial and satellite data, 3D web graphics, game design, AI, interface design and cloud deployment. We work like a small mission team: everyone owns a part, we review each other’s work, and we check every number against a real source. We’re curious, learn fast, and care about making things that are both accurate and fun.
summary:
Mars missions are slow, dangerous and unpredictable. A message to Earth can take over 20 minutes each way, and in 2009 NASA’s Spirit rover ended its mission trapped in soft sand. No single planner, human or AI, can test every possible path. So we asked: what if everyone could help?

We built Marswalk Planner, an interactive 3D map of Mars and a crowdsourced mission simulator. Our planner combines more than ten NASA and ESA datasets (terrain, ground firmness, minerals, weather and radiation) and, from a plain-language goal like “find clay where water once flowed”, plans a safe landing spot and routes checked for oxygen, storm shelter and the walk home.

Then anyone can play that mission. Players redraw the route, drive it in first person and race an AI driver. Our server re-scores every run on the same real terrain and physics, so scores can’t be faked, and ranks it on a shared leaderboard. Every run adds a verified route: the best human routes become the benchmark our AI must beat, and the data to improve it.

This turns people’s competitive streak into safer routes on Mars.
details:
Our big idea: crowdsourcing safer routes on Mars. No single planner, human or computer, can test every possible path across Mars, so Marswalk Planner lets anyone help. First, our planner builds a safe mission from real NASA data. Then anyone can play that same mission as a first-person game: redraw the route to try to beat it, and drive it with a helmet display that shows oxygen and the path ahead. To make every run trustworthy, the player’s browser never reports its own score. Our server replays each route over the same real terrain, with the same physics the planner uses, and rejects anything the terrain would not allow. The results board then compares the player with an AI driver, both on the player’s route and on the planner’s original route, along with oxygen, energy, distance and cost, and ranks the run on a shared leaderboard. Every run adds a verified, scored route. Together they grow into a crowdsourced collection of the most efficient paths: a benchmark our AI has to beat, and the data to make it better. People are naturally competitive, and we turn that competitiveness into safer routes for future astronauts.

What it does. Marswalk Planner is an interactive 3D map of Mars combined with a mission simulator. It helps an astronaut plan a Marswalk, a trip outside the base on foot or by rover, by answering three questions before every trip: where should I go to reach my science goal, how do I get there safely, and what happens if something goes wrong? The astronaut first finds a place, either by typing a name like Jezero or Olympus Mons or simply by looking at it on the globe. Then they type a goal in everyday words, for example “find clay where water once flowed”. Helmut, the planner’s AI assistant, asks only for what is still missing, such as the time of day and whether the crew will walk or drive. The planner then returns a safe landing spot, the places that best match the goal, and up to three possible routes. For each route it shows the distance, the travel time, how much oxygen or battery power it uses, how many minutes it would take to reach shelter in a dust storm, and whether the crew could walk home if their vehicle broke down. The crew can watch the route play out on the map, stand on the ground at eye height to see what the astronaut would see, or hand the mission to the game described above.

How it works. Behind the map is what we call a data cube: for each area, more than ten NASA and ESA datasets are lined up on the same grid, so every point on the map holds all of its values at once, including height, steepness, how firm the ground is, which minerals are present, how bright and how warm the surface is, and the radiation dose. This is what lets the planner ask questions that combine many kinds of data at once. Ground firmness comes from thermal inertia, which measures how quickly the surface heats up and cools down; NASA’s THEMIS and TES instruments measured it from orbit. Loose sand changes temperature quickly, while solid rock changes slowly, and loose sand is exactly the kind of ground that trapped the Spirit rover in 2009. Minerals that form in water, such as clays and carbonates, come from the CRISM instrument, which identifies minerals by the colours of light they reflect. Next, the planner turns these layers into a travel-cost map that says how long it takes to cross each spot: it uses a well-known model of walking speed on hills for astronauts and NASA’s wheel-slip measurements from the Curiosity rover for vehicles, adds extra cost for loose sand and rough ground, and blocks anything too steep. The best route is the quickest safe path across that map, found with a standard shortest-path algorithm. Oxygen use is adjusted for every uphill and downhill stretch, using a published model of how much energy walking on slopes takes, and must stay within NASA’s planned oxygen supply for a Mars spacesuit with a safety reserve left over. A second map measures how far every point is from shelter. Finally, the options are scored in a decision matrix that weighs science value, safety, resources used, travel time, landing quality and how much we trust the data, and Helmut explains in plain words why the best option won. The game’s scoring uses this same terrain and physics, which is why a player’s route and the planner’s route can be compared fairly.

Benefits. Today, deciding where to walk on Mars means comparing separate maps of terrain, minerals, temperature and radiation by hand. Marswalk Planner brings them together on one screen, plans with all of them at once, and shows its reasoning. Every number can be traced back to the dataset or study it came from, layers that are calculated rather than measured are clearly labelled, and the safety checks a crew would otherwise have to do by hand are done automatically for every route. The crowdsourced game adds something no single planner has: many independent attempts at the same problem, each one checked by the same rules. It uses plain language that anyone can follow, while experts can reveal the technical details with one key, and it runs in any web browser, with nothing to install.

Intended impact. Future astronauts on Mars will have to plan and re-plan their trips on the spot, because waiting for Earth takes too long. We want to show what their planning tool could look like: one that combines real data, explains its choices, keeps safety margins in plain view, and gets better as more people test it. By opening mission planning to students and the public, the same tool turns curiosity about Mars into a shared, growing search for better and safer routes.

How it is creative. Most Mars maps only display data, and most route planners work alone. Ours plans with the data, can be talked to like a teammate, and invites the public to compete against it on fair, server-checked terms, so people’s competitive streak produces useful routes. We treated Mars the way a doctor’s software treats a medical scan, where every pixel carries measurements, so questions that combine many datasets can be answered point by point. And we let the crew see the same plan three ways: from orbit, from the ground at eye height, and from the driver’s seat.

Factors we considered. Fairness came first for the crowdsourcing: every score is recalculated on our server, so a leaderboard entry always means a route that really works on the measured terrain. Safety came first for the planning: the planner keeps an oxygen and battery reserve (a larger one in dust-storm season), never lands right on top of the target, checks the time to shelter and the walk home, and warns when the sun is low. Honesty about the data mattered just as much: we used published NASA figures wherever they exist, labelled our own assumptions, and stated our limits, such as map detail of about 116 m per pixel outside Jezero, which is too coarse to show individual boulders, and that player rankings do not yet feed back into the planner automatically. We made the AI safe by design: it can only press the same buttons a person can, it never calculates the routes itself, and the built-in assistant works even without an AI service. We designed for real people, with a map-first layout where each button opens one tool, a manual and tips, support for keyboards and screen readers, reduced motion, phones and slower connections, and areas that load only when needed so the app stays fast.

Tools we used. The back end is written in Python, using FastAPI for the web server, NumPy and SciPy for the calculations, rasterio and GDAL to read and align the map data, scikit-image for route finding, Matplotlib and Pillow to draw map images, and SQLite to save plans, attempts and rankings. The front end is JavaScript, HTML and CSS built on CesiumJS, an open-source 3D globe, set up for Mars, with Web Audio for sounds. The live app runs on Cloudflare Pages, with the planning server on AWS Lightsail, packaged with Docker. We worked in Git and GitHub with one branch per teammate and a written changelog for every merged change, designed the interface in Figma, and used AI coding assistants, as described in our AI disclosure. No special hardware is needed: it runs on any laptop or phone with a web browser.
